name: Adam Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the junior shepherd on Carn Ridge, which is about two thousand acres of hill grazing run by a community land trust, so the village owns it together. We've got roughly nine hundred ewes, mostly hardy hill breeds, out on the open hill most of the year. A normal day in November is checking the tups, the rams, are doing their job, moving groups between fields with the dogs, and fixing walls that the weather knocked down. I'm on the quad bike or on foot up the hill until about four, when the light goes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it at forty-something?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a postman for nineteen years, the round up the valley, and I got to know every farm on it. When the post office cut the round to three days a week, the trust advertised for a trainee shepherd and I thought, why not. My head shepherd, Morag, has been doing this since she was six. She's patient with me, mostly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the dogs, and I like being up there when the cloud lifts off the tops and you can see three valleys. What wears me out is lambing, five weeks of no proper sleep in April. And the pay, which is less than the post paid. My wife Lena's a nurse at the cottage hospital, and she's really what keeps the mortgage paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say brilliant, more of it. I already use AI every day, mostly on my phone, to check what a ewe's symptoms might mean before I bother Morag. I'd be the one posting about how useful it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it's like having a second, very well-read shepherd in my pocket, one who's never actually seen a sheep. It helps me learn faster, which I need. But a better search engine doesn't climb the hill for you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, but more. I'd set up a proper record of every ewe with the AI helping me sort it, lambing dates, which ones had trouble, which ones are lame every winter. I'd show Morag, and she'd pretend not to be impressed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. I like new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Morag actually think of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks it's a toy for people who don't know their own sheep. But last winter the phone helped me spot early signs of twin lamb disease, and she said, well, maybe keep the toy. That's high praise from Morag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it help with money at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, not yet. It saved us a vet call once, maybe eighty pounds, because I caught a problem early. But my wage is my wage, the AI doesn't get me paid more for knowing more.

S0.say: I'd say brilliant, more of it. I already use AI every day on my phone to check what a ewe's symptoms might mean, and I'd be the one posting about how useful it is.
S0.think: For me it's like a well-read second shepherd in my pocket who's never seen a sheep. It helps me learn faster, but it doesn't climb the hill for me.
S0.do: Sets up a full record of every ewe with AI help, tracking lambing dates and problems. Shows it to Morag, his head shepherd, hoping she'll use it.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit excited, because he likes new things.
S0.quote: It's like having a second, very well-read shepherd in my pocket, one who's never actually seen a sheep.
S0.fieldNote: Adam is cheerful and talkative, an early adopter in a very traditional corner of farming. He uses AI to make up for being new, and his head shepherd's grudging approval clearly matters to him. Money came up only through his wife's nursing wage, which he openly credits with keeping the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the trust should keep training people like me, and push the government to pay for it. If farms stop taking beginners, the hills empty out. You can already drive through valleys where there's no one under fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think slow change is fine for me. I'm keen on the tools, so I'd keep ahead of it. What worries me is that I'm the last trainee they'll take, and then it's Morag and me forever, and then just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn to fly a drone for checking sheep on the far tops, the trust has talked about one for a year. I'd get the licence over winter, about two hundred quid, which we'd have to find. And I'd ask the trust to take on a school leaver as well, because someone has to learn from Morag after I've learned from her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more about the valley than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does two hundred pounds come from, in your house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, probably Christmas. We'd tell Noah and Ruby it's a smaller one this year. Lena would say fine but you're doing the cooking, which is fair, she does enough twelve-hour shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does a school leaver matter so much to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Morag will retire one day and everything in her head goes with her. I'm forty-three, I'm not the future, I'm the bridge. Someone eighteen needs to be standing on the other end of it.

S1.say: I'd say the trust should keep training people like me, and push the government to pay for it. Without beginners the hills empty out, and some valleys already have no one under fifty.
S1.think: Slow change suits me, because I'm keen on the tools and I'd keep ahead. What worries me is being the last trainee the trust ever takes on.
S1.do: Gets a drone licence over winter for about two hundred pounds to check sheep on the far tops. Urges the trust to take on a school leaver too.
S1.feel: Uneasy, more about the valley than about himself.
S1.quote: What worries me is that I'm the last trainee they'll take, and then it's Morag and me forever, and then just me.
S1.fieldNote: He thinks about the community more than his own job, which fits both his politics and the land trust setting. He's ready to spend money he doesn't have on learning, and the family pays through a smaller Christmas. He came back twice to the idea of someone younger learning from Morag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance to share the gains properly, like the trust does with the land. If computers do the paperwork, cut the working week, don't cut the workers. I'd post that and probably get shouted at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be curious about the new AI jobs. I'm good with this stuff and I'm on low pay. But they'd be in cities, and I don't want to leave the hill, so mostly it's just interesting from a distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer the trust a deal: let the AI do the grant forms and the movement records, the paperwork that tracks every sheep that comes and goes, and let me run it, so the office lady keeps her hours for the harder stuff. I'd spend evenings learning the farm subsidy rules with AI help. And I'd keep on at the drone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit uneasy for the people in offices. Lena's hospital admin team would worry me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get shouted at online. By whom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Pete, mainly, he's got opinions about everything and they're all the opposite of mine. He'd say I want to share out other people's money. I'd say, Pete, you've never shared a sandwich in your life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Lena's job be touched?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The nursing, no, someone still has to put a drip in. But the ward clerks and the people who book appointments, maybe. Lena says half her shift is typing anyway, so maybe she'd get some of it back, as long as they don't cut a nurse to pay for the software.

S2.say: I'd say it's a chance to share gains, like the trust shares the land. Cut the working week, not the workers.
S2.think: I'd be curious about the new AI jobs, since I'm good with the tools and on low pay. But they'd be in cities, and I don't want to leave the hill.
S2.do: Proposes running the trust's AI-assisted paperwork, such as grant forms and sheep movement records. Spends evenings learning subsidy rules with AI help and keeps working toward the drone.
S2.feel: Mostly calm, a bit uneasy for office workers and his wife's hospital admin colleagues.
S2.quote: I'd say, Pete, you've never shared a sandwich in your life.
S2.fieldNote: He sees office automation partly as an opening for himself, and partly as a political question about sharing. He won't leave the hill, which caps how far his adaptability can take him. He enjoyed telling the story about his cousin and was clearly at ease in this scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when you need public ownership, of land, of housing, of the AI if it comes to that. Look at our trust: the village owns the hill and nobody gets rich, but nobody gets kicked off either. I'd go on every march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, house prices booming would be awful for our valley. Holiday homes would eat every cottage. Our two will never afford to live where they grew up, and that bothers me more than my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer with the trust to build some affordable homes on trust land, we've talked about four houses by the old school. I'd use AI to help with the planning paperwork, which is a monster. I'd also take any extra shepherding work going on the neighbouring hills, at about ninety a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not for the reason you'd think. I'm fine. It's the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noah and Ruby about where they'll live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm trying to build them a house, which is true and also a bit of a joke between us. Noah would ask if it'll have a games room. Ruby would ask if the dog can come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're fine. With under a month saved, are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. One broken quad bike and we're on the credit card, and the trust's quad is older than Noah. So, fine-ish, as long as nothing breaks, which on a hill farm is never.

S3.say: I'd say this is exactly when you need public ownership of land, housing and maybe AI. The trust shows that nobody gets rich but nobody gets kicked off.
S3.think: Booming house prices would turn our valley into holiday homes. Noah and Ruby might never afford to live where they grew up, and that bothers me more than my job.
S3.do: Volunteers with the trust to build four affordable homes on trust land, using AI to help with planning paperwork. Takes extra shepherding on nearby hills at about ninety a day.
S3.feel: Anxious, not for himself but for the valley.
S3.quote: Our two will never afford to live where they grew up, and that bothers me more than my job.
S3.fieldNote: His worry moved almost entirely from work to housing and the next generation. He offered a concrete local fix rather than a slogan. When I gently raised his thin savings, he admitted one broken quad bike would sink them, which sat oddly beside his claim to be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots should be owned by the community, like our hill. If a robot shepherd works the trust land, the money it saves goes back to the village, not to some company. I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm torn. Robots on flat farms, sure, but on our hill, in the cloud and the bog and the scree? I'd give them a winter. But if they do cope, the trust would be daft not to use one, and then there's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be the one who runs the robots, not the one replaced by them. I'd ask the trust for training the first month it's even talked about, and I'd learn every manual. And I'd keep the dogs, because I don't believe a robot gathers a hill in fog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, swinging to excited. I can't tell which one wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the trust would be daft not to use one. Then what about you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's down to whether the trust is what it says it is. If the village owns the robot and keeps me on to run it, that's the dream. If they sell my job to save money, then all that talk about community was just talk, and I'd say so at the meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Morag say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say she'll retire the day a robot brings a ewe down off the ridge in a blizzard, and she'd mean it. Then she'd quietly ask me to show her how it works. She's always more curious than she lets on.

S4.say: I'd say robots should be owned by the community, like the hill. Savings from a robot shepherd should go back to the village, not a company.
S4.think: I'm torn. I doubt robots can cope with the cloud, bog and scree on our hill, but if they do, the trust would use one, and then there's me.
S4.do: Asks the trust for robot training the first month it's discussed and learns every manual. Keeps the dogs, doubting robots can gather a hill in fog.
S4.feel: Anxious, swinging toward excited, and he can't tell which wins.
S4.quote: If they sell my job to save money, then all that talk about community was just talk, and I'd say so at the meeting.
S4.fieldNote: Unusually for a hands-on worker, his mood didn't jump much in the robot scenario, because he wants to run the machines. His faith in the trust is being tested and he knows it. He put the question to himself before I had to, which says a lot about how he thinks.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, three, because of the houses. Robots I can maybe ride. What would help is the trust, and others like it, being allowed to buy land and build homes for local people before the money gets there first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the dogs. Every time someone talks about robots on farms they forget there's already a smart worker on the hill that isn't a person, and it's a collie called Bess. We've been working alongside clever helpers for hundreds of years.

headlineQuote: Our two will never afford to live where they grew up, and that bothers me more than my job.
portrait: Adam Moreau is 43, a former postman now training as a junior shepherd on hill land owned by a village land trust. He is married to Lena, a nurse whose wage keeps the mortgage paid, and they have two children and almost no savings. He uses AI daily and treats each scenario as something to learn, from a ewe database to drone checks to running robots himself. His sharpest worry isn't his own job but booming house prices emptying the valley of local families, and he trusts community ownership to share whatever gains come.
biggestWorry: The fast scenario worries him most, because booming house prices would turn the valley into holiday homes and price out his children.
whatWouldHelp: Letting the land trust and groups like it buy land and build homes for local people before outside money gets there first.
